title: Sticky inflation, cooling housing: RBA's rates dilemma
full_text:
Property The economy has been too reliant on the easy money gains from housing, so a rebalancing could reallocate labour into more productive areas.
The Reserve Bank of Australia is facing an unusual conundrum of sticky inflation and falling house prices.
Inflation and house prices do not often move in the opposite direction in Australia. It is rare for home prices to fall in this property-obsessed nation.
The day before the latest inflation figures were published on Wednesday, RBA governor Michele Bullock said inflation was "still too high".
Bullock also said the central bank was closely watching the housing market and admitted conditions were weaker than the RBA had expected. "The housing market is a bit of a litmus test in some sense," Bullock said on Tuesday.
To be sure, inflation is the immediate priority for the RBA. The consumer price index released on Wednesday was not as bad as feared. Headline inflation eased a bit to 3.8 per cent.
The RBA's preferred measure of underlying inflation, which strips out the most volatile price changes, printed at 3.6 per cent for the June quarter, below the RBA's 3.8 per cent forecast.
The swift reaction by financial markets was to rule out an immediate interest rate rise in August and reduce the chance of a fourth rate hike in 2026 to about 50-50.
Nonetheless, inflation remains well above the RBA's 2 per cent to 3 per cent target band.
Home-grown inflation is elevated, as evidenced by strong price pressures in domestic market services inflation and non-tradable items.
The labour market is tight, underlined by a low 4.4 per cent unemployment rate and stagnant labour productivity.
Conflict in the Middle East is not over, and fuel price pressures could re-emerge.
Further monetary policy tightening in the months ahead should not be dismissed and interest rate cuts appear to be a long way off.
"The board is prepared to act as required to achieve its mandate, including increasing the cash rate further if needed," Bullock said on Tuesday.
But the weakening housing market may help do some of the RBA's inflation-fighting.
The RBA's three previous interest rate rises and the Albanese government's tax changes to negative gearing and capital gains have had a chilling effect on the housing market.
Property prices are falling in Sydney and Melbourne. Analysts are tipping house prices to fall as much as 5 per cent to 10 per cent from their lofty peaks in the two largest markets. Home price growth in other capital cities is rapidly cooling.
Auction clearance rates have declined to around 50 per cent, well below the 70-plus per cent before the budget tax changes and interest rate rises.
Loans to investors have dried up, and other buyers are holding back as they sense home prices have further to fall.
When asset prices fall, consumers feel less wealthy and typically spend a bit less.
When house prices last fell in 2019, RBA research suggested a negative wealth effect would reduce spending on new cars, furniture and clothing, reversing previous increases in spending on these categories when house prices were rising strongly.
Softer consumer spending reduces inflation pressures.
Bullock said the bank was looking for "flow on effects" from the weaker housing market and consumer spending was already slowing.
Falling house prices and elevated interest rates will discourage property developers from building new homes because they will find it harder to make a profit.
Owners will similarly be less inclined to spend money on renovations. Over time, fewer homes being built and renovated will reduce work for builders and tradies.
The weaker demand for these housing-connected workers will reduce their incomes, employment and spending.
Real estate agents, bankers, mortgage brokers, removalists, buyer agents, property advertisers, valuers and conveyancers will also feel the pinch from the reduction in the number of homes being bought and sold due to the government's tax changes.
Existing investors with "grandfathered" negatively geared properties are likely to hang on to these prized homes for longer and avoid selling.
To be sure, the RBA is not worried from a financial stability perspective about house prices easing back to their early 2026 peaks.
Less than 1 per cent of borrowers are in negative equity because of price falls and most borrowers are ahead on their mortgages and have considerable savings buffers. "The easing in established housing prices has so far been modest, following a period of strong growth" and "monetary policy doesn't target housing prices," Bullock said.
Nonetheless, the RBA is paying attention to the broader economic effects of the housing slowdown.
Arguably, the Australian economy has been too reliant on the easy money gains from housing, so a rebalancing could reallocate labour into more productive areas.
John Kehoe is economics editor at The Australian Financial Review.
